talks.title: Framework-led Cyber Security
talks.teaser: Shows how a security framework and maturity scoring give organisations a shared language to plan, measure and fund security.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that many organisations still respond to threats reactively, buying tools and plugging holes as problems surface. The speaker, drawing on a defensive background, proposes adopting a security framework as a common language that lets technical teams explain their work to management, boards and budget holders. He notes that frameworks such as the NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework, Cyber Essentials, NIST and CIS controls share much common ground, so picking one as a base and adapting it is more practical than chasing all of them.

Drawing on his time at a university, he describes overlaying a CMMI-style maturity model, scored from zero to five, onto the Cyber Assessment Framework's pass or fail indicators. This gave clearer targets, year-on-year charts and a way to link projects, from short fixes to multi-year identity work, back to the framework. Risk-based prioritisation, with a short list of top risks such as ransomware, patching and business email compromise, helped justify budget. In questions he suggested gamified leaderboards to motivate departments, involving finance and HR to test whether controls really work, and mapping several standards together to consolidate audits.

The takeaway is that a framework gives direction and measurement but still has to be adapted to the business, and that checkbox compliance hides real gaps. Practitioners should treat the framework as a base to modify, measure progress against it over time, and keep business leaders involved in deciding priorities.

talks.title: Cybersecurity, Cyberpunk, And Dreams Of Electric Sheep
talks.teaser: Compares cybersecurity marketing films with cyberpunk stories using narrative theory, focusing on heroes and plot twists.
talks.summary:
This talk presents a small research project that began with a collection of around 26 short films made by cybersecurity vendors and consultancies between about 2014 and 2018. Each film is under 15 minutes, high budget and follows a story. To study them, the speaker combined a structural method from a 1928 study of folktales with a French semiotician's five codes for reading a text, coding each shot. A comparison set of cyberpunk short films was analysed the same way.

The comparison shows shared features: both genres feature hackers, IT staff and large organisations. The security videos fall into three recurring story types, one built around a hacker hero, one around an IT professional and one around an ordinary worker helped by a security firm. In these films the protagonist is whoever holds and reveals the most knowledge, while cyberpunk protagonists tend to conceal information. Plot twists in the security videos usually confirm who holds power, and criminal and ethical hackers are almost interchangeable.

The speaker concludes that the security videos are highly formulaic and that the stories the industry tells about itself shape how practitioners see their roles and who gets heard. Attendees are encouraged to notice the narratives they tell about hacking and whose voices dominate them. The talk ends with a call for red teamers, pentesters, bug bounty hunters and social engineers to join ongoing research on the professionalization of hacking.

talks.title: Why Your Pen Test Didn’t Matter
talks.teaser: Explores why pentest findings get diluted or accepted instead of fixed, and how reports can drive real risk reduction.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that a penetration test often has less lasting effect than its authors expect. Speaker Tim Holman, a long-time consultant, describes a recurring pattern: after a test, findings are debated, reclassified as lower risk, or accepted so the audit passes, while the underlying weakness stays in place. He ties this to incentives, with security teams measured on closed findings and management looking at a risk register that seems manageable.

Holman walks through how reports lose their meaning. Technical findings such as weak LDAP signing do not obviously show the path to domain admin, and scanner output can bury a critical issue, such as a Subversion server exposing database credentials, near the bottom of a list. He notes that attackers chain several lower-rated issues, such as excessive delegation and forgotten service accounts, into a compromise, which CVSS scores alone miss. He also criticises annual testing as a snapshot, acquisitions that go untested, and continuous pentesting sold by vendors that is largely vulnerability scanning with monitoring.

For practitioners, the advice is to write each finding around the risk: why the customer should care, how an attacker would use it, what to fix first, and what happens if it is ignored. Reports should be shorter, use plain language, and avoid copied boilerplate. Testers should hold their severity ratings under pressure, and organisations should ask whether a fix actually removed an attack path rather than just closing a ticket.

talks.title: What Trading Systems Taught Me About Breaking (And Defending) Infrastructure
talks.teaser: Shows how timing races, parser mismatches and state-machine gaps break distributed systems, using lessons from trading firms.
talks.summary:
The speaker draws on years spent on options market-making desks, where a timing-based attack by a faster rival drained money from the firm. The talk argues that such failures often sit not inside one component but in the gaps between components of a distributed system. Two individually valid requests arriving close together can break a rule that no single check enforces, and a simple bank-balance withdrawal is used to illustrate the idea.

The talk groups the hostile conditions into time, state, input and evidence. Examples include retries colliding with legitimate requests, low-priority work clogging higher-priority operations, and two parsers reading the same message in different orders. An authentication flow was shown where a refresh token racing a logout can keep a session alive, and where a transition skipped an MFA pending state because the design never named it. The speaker also questioned relying on CAPTCHA and MFA as the only controls.

For defenders, the recommendations centre on defining invariants and explicit states, parsing and canonicalising input once, and guarding and testing transitions rather than only the happy path. Logs should be kept independent of administrators and made tamper-evident, for example by hashing linked events and signing them. Deterministic incident replay is presented as the strongest form of evidence.

talks.title: 5 Years Of Security Lessons Or The Choose-Your-Own-Adventure That Broke Reality
talks.teaser: Revisits five years of audience-picked security topics, from careers and incident response to risk, communication and choosing tools.
talks.summary:
Dave McKenzie explains that this talk began as a last-minute request to fill a slot and grew into a format where the audience picked numbered questions and he answered each one live over about three years. Looking back, he grouped the questions into themes such as careers, risk, incident response, ethics, technology and breaking into the field, and noted that the answers often went somewhere other than the audience expected.

On careers, he argued that technical skill matters less than being able to communicate with the business, that people who judge you for how you look or talk stop listening, and that researching a company's risk profile helps in interviews. He warned about false urgency, burnout and poor professional branding. On incident response, he judged the worst case by its human impact rather than its cost, stressed that incident management is about people under pressure, and urged varied tabletop exercises that force decisions under uncertainty. He also argued that compliance such as PCI DSS is a business requirement rather than real protection, and that budget guidance differs between typical firms and heavily regulated ones.

He closed by saying that tools matter less than understanding the problem they solve, that people should learn new technology enough to see how it fits together, and that being useful and kind to colleagues does more for a career than chasing the latest tool. The takeaway is that security work is mostly about helping the business do its job.

talks.title: Adversary
talks.teaser: Walks through how attackers move from a laptop into hybrid Entra ID and SharePoint estates, and why defenders see little.
talks.summary:
Neil Lines argues that the move from traditional Active Directory to cloud identity has changed what a red team can do after being handed a standard laptop. Hardened endpoints have given way to fresh builds under zero trust, and typical hybrid estates pair a VPN with a username, password and MFA. The talk shows how a VPN client can be fetched from its vendor and how a successful Microsoft 365 sign-in can hint at weak conditional access.

The middle of the talk covers tradecraft. A browser-in-the-middle tool relays a user's login so the password, MFA token and session are captured and then taken over, and a colleague's tool reduces that setup to minutes. Calls to service desks are used to have MFA methods re-registered. On file shares and SharePoint, keyword searches for words like password or service account names surface credentials, while domain user lists and network diagrams turn up the same way. Company portals and Visual Studio Code extensions are shown as installation routes that need no admin rights, and a VMDK file opened with 7-Zip yields registry hives whose hashes are cracked offline.

The closing section points to visibility gaps, since EDR may see little of what runs inside an installed hypervisor or extension, and audit search logs take hours to become available. The practical lessons are to review SharePoint permissions, control which applications users can install, and tighten how service desks verify identity before resetting credentials.

talks.title: Post-startup (security) Growing Pains "Hi, It's Me, I'm The Risk"
talks.teaser: A candid rant on why startups grow without security in mind, and how people, identity, devices and bus factor become risks.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at companies in the startup maturity phase and how security tends to be left out as they grow. Maya Boeckh contrasts the business-school idea of a startup, a lifecycle running from problem to product to scale, with a looser view of a small business built around an idea. The rant then turns to priorities: funding, a product that appears to work, operating costs and fixing outages tend to win over security.

The central argument is that security is a two-body problem of people and computers, and both are hard. An identity provider with centralised federation and conditional access can help, but data is easy to copy and very hard to recall once it has been sent. Other points include password reuse between personal and corporate accounts, the trust tiers around staff, and bring-your-own-device setups that leave companies without guardrails. Two European Commission projects, an IoT smart home security project and a vehicle network project, were cloned and reworked in about four months after staff changed. A supplier's daily database dump sat in an unsecured cloud storage bucket, which the speaker found and disclosed. MFA prompts and removed local admin rights brought their own friction for remote workers and slow sync delays.

The closing advice is to look for the smallest steps with the largest impact, such as an email rule that blocks certain domains, rather than adding more tooling. Two takeaways stand out: security is a cost that many startups do not treat as part of their objective, and anyone who could leave or become unavailable, the bus factor, belongs in the threat model.

talks.title: Hacking Stripe Integrations To Bypass E-Commerce Payments
talks.teaser: Walks through logic flaws in Stripe payment integrations that let attackers reuse saved cards and skip payment.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how Stripe payment integrations on e-commerce sites can be abused. The speaker began with a bug bounty competition that had Stripe in scope. After little turned up in Stripe's main dashboard, they turned to the in-scope GitHub repositories and a Magento extension that adds Stripe payments to online stores.

The walkthrough covers four issues. Saved-card payment method IDs followed a pattern that could be guessed, and the Magento backend took the customer from the payment method rather than from the logged-in account, so one user could charge another user's saved card. An Amazon Pay express checkout shipping endpoint accepted any amount, because the server only checked that the payment status was successful. Orders could also be created before payment completed, and the amount-mismatch check ran before the status check, so the order went through with an overpayment message instead of an unpaid status. Last, a Stripe API endpoint for retrieving saved card details required only the merchant's public key and no authentication, exposing card and billing data.

Each flaw was fixed by adding an ownership, amount, status or authentication check. The main takeaway is that complex integrations can hide simple logic bugs, and that values coming from the client, such as IDs, amounts and payment status, should be verified on the server before an order or charge is accepted.

talks.title: Living Off The Web Of Lies
talks.teaser: Shows how red teams abuse free tiers and trusted email and signing services to build hard-to-attribute phishing infrastructure.
talks.summary:
James Williams argues that red teams can hide behind widely trusted third-party services, since large email, hosting and document providers are almost impossible for organisations to block. He lays out the aims: avoid attribution by the blue team and the providers, stop separate engagements from crossing paths, and keep operator identities compartmentalised. Persona identities are arranged in layers, from cheap disposable accounts up to real or company identities that are costly to replace.

The middle of the talk covers building persona accounts, including names, phone numbers, email addresses, payment methods and photos, and growing a believable LinkedIn profile over time. He then walks through examples using free tiers and trials. Cloudflare's free email routing and a captcha in front of landing pages, a free mass-mailing account, and a free document-signing trial that can carry a link to an attacker-controlled URL are shown, along with each service's limits and the account-termination risks when activity is reported. He also shares a passive Burp Suite approach for capturing LinkedIn search results without automating the platform.

He closes with advice for each side. Red teams should vary their techniques so campaigns do not become a recognisable indicator. Defenders should check DNS TXT records for the services their staff use, cover abused trials in awareness training, test how users and report-phish buttons respond, and agree how vendors handle abuse reports.

talks.title: Scams, Sextortion And Snapchats: Keeping Gen-Alpha Safe In A Digital Wild West
talks.teaser: A conference session surveys Gen Alpha sextortion and scam patterns on social apps, plus parent, school, and regulatory responses.
talks.summary:
The presenter frames Gen Alpha as always online from infancy, skilled with devices yet unprepared for predators who exploit validation needs, instant gratification, and platform features such as disappearing messages. Audience members describe school sextortion cases, personal blackmail attempts, and risky youth-focused apps without verification.

The talk walks through real U.S. and U.K. fatalities and FBI reporting volumes, then typical grooming paths: compliments, shared interests, sexualized chats on Snapchat or WhatsApp, screenshot blackmail, urgency, and shame. Parallel scenarios cover gaming gift scams, fake Roblox generators, and influencer impersonation stealing bank details. Matthew Falder’s U.K. case illustrates large-scale extortion. Predator psychology is tied to isolation, urgency, and reputation threats, with warning signs like withdrawal and anxiety.

Later sections map the U.K. Online Safety Act and GDPR to platform duties and weak enforcement, then practical guidance: red flags, judgment-free check-ins, parental controls, emergency protocols, digital citizenship in schools, safety-by-design for developers, and initiatives such as Friends Against Scams. The close urges one honest conversation with a young person, learning one platform they use, and one concrete safety step.

talks.title: Threat Modelling: How I Learned To Stop Worrying And Love Misconfigurations
talks.teaser: Explains how threat modelling with STRIDE and DREAD helps teams catch cloud misconfigurations at design time.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that many recent breaches come from misconfiguration rather than zero-day flaws, and that insecure defaults, such as shared access keys on Azure storage, leave teams exposed. The speakers link this to alert fatigue and to developers who prioritise getting systems working over building them securely.

They present threat modelling as a practical habit. Teams sketch a data flow diagram, mark the trust boundaries where an attacker could act, and apply STRIDE to each element. PASTA and DREAD are covered as alternatives, with DREAD used to turn technical severity into plain-language impact statements that developers can act on. A live demo shows Microsoft's Threat Modeling Tool with custom stencils, threat templates, mitigation states and report export.

The closing advice is to use threat models to plan pentests and to confirm that mitigations and logging work, since repeated findings often show fixes that were never carried through. Attendees are told to ask after each exercise whether it was effective and whether the team would repeat it, and are pointed to the threat modelling manifesto and to resources for diagrams and icons.

talks.title: Statistical Inconspicuousness
talks.teaser: Shows how static features like entropy, imports and code signing make red team implants stand out from goodware.
talks.summary:
Two red team operators present preliminary findings from a study comparing red team implants and loaders against known malware and against legitimate Windows and third-party software. They gathered samples from public malware collections, hash-matched downloads and package installers, then extracted static properties from each portable executable in the way the Ember dataset does. The goal was to see which properties machine learning detections would notice before anything runs.

The talk walks through several features. Entropy is the first: encrypted or packed malware sits close to the top of the scale, while goodware clusters in a narrow middle band, and a plain Meterpreter payload stood out clearly. File size showed a line below which almost all of the goodware and Windows binaries did not fall, so very small loaders and heavily bloated ones both looked unusual. Imports were compared across samples, and dynamically resolving Win32 functions reduced the visible list of suspicious calls, though it still differed from ordinary software. Code signing was common in goodware but stolen or expired certificates were prominent in malware. Compiler identification via Rich headers showed MSVC dominating legitimate software, and packers added section names that rarely appear in normal binaries.

The speakers close with practical advice: take care with entropy, size, imports, signing and compiler choice, use kill switches and environment keying, and avoid stolen certificates. Their main conclusion is that mimicking Windows binaries takes real effort, while blending in with ordinary third-party software is more achievable. They noted that a simple import-based model already performed well in early tests, and that the full paper is still in progress.

talks.title: We're Still So Serial!
talks.teaser: Covers finding and weaponizing .NET deserialization gadget chains in Windows binaries, and the telemetry they leave behind.
talks.summary:
The talk covers .NET object serialization and how deserializing untrusted data can lead to code execution, with a focus on using this in red team engagements. It explains the basics of serialization formats such as XML, JSON and binary, and how a gadget chain runs code when an object is rebuilt. A demo shows a payload that launches a process, and the speaker notes that spawning child processes is easily spotted by endpoint tools, so running code inside an already trusted process is preferred.

To find targets, the speaker scans endpoints for .NET binaries, searches their code for unsafe deserialization calls, and then traces whether user-supplied data can reach them. He discusses Microsoft-signed Windows binaries with usable paths and a JSON.NET case in an Azure service. He also covers a Microsoft patch that blocks a common file-based gadget chain, a known bypass for that patch, and reflection for calling existing methods in loaded assemblies. Operational concerns include random assembly names, gaps in ETW telemetry, and AMSI and antivirus detections of staged payloads.

For defenders, unexpected in-memory assemblies with random names, or unusual loads of the workflow component model, are useful signals to hunt for. The speaker also describes a client that removed the PowerShell engine DLL from a sandbox, which broke many of the gadget chains.

talks.title: My GRITT OS: Good Resilience In Testing Times Operating System
talks.teaser: Explores burnout in cyber security and the personal routines, from sleep to creative hobbies, that help keep resilience up.
talks.summary:
Mo Amin describes his own experience of nearly burning out while working as a freelance security consultant. At one point he was juggling around 20 projects, several of them high profile, and was pulled between project managers, colleagues and political pressures. He explains how his routines slipped during that period: his walking, diet and sleep suffered, and he kept thinking about work at home and over weekends.

He reviews burnout research, noting that much of the early material comes from healthcare and describes exhaustion, cynicism and a sense of low personal accomplishment. He points to a study of healthcare workers in Singapore and a report suggesting security professionals in Australia show burnout levels similar to healthcare. He argues the industry rarely discusses this and asks how resilient security strategies can rest on people who are already burnt out. Shift work, fixed hours and unequal pay come up in audience questions.

His coping approach, which he calls an operating system, rests on diet, exercise and sleep as a foundation, with travel and time outdoors, creative hobbies away from screens, a support network and meaningful work built on top. He closes by saying wellbeing is each person's own responsibility, that organisations could do more, that toxic environments are worth leaving, and that asking for help matters.

talks.title: Tales Of DOMinica
talks.teaser: Shows how to find DOM-based cross-site scripting by tracing sources to sinks, including filter bypasses that scanners often miss.
talks.summary:
DOM-based cross-site scripting differs from reflected and stored variants because the payload is injected by client-side JavaScript after the page loads, so server-side scanning often misses it. The talk treats exploitation as a method: find a source where user input enters JavaScript, find a sink where that input is handled unsafely, and then find a way to connect the two.

The speaker starts with a basic case where a script element written through innerHTML does not run, so an image tag with an invalid source and an onerror handler is used instead. A second case writes user input into an image source that passes through encodeURI. The encoding blocks spaces and double quotes but leaves single quotes alone, so a single quote closes the string and lets an alert fire. In this case the payload never appears in the server response, so a standard reflected-payload intruder scan finds nothing. A third lab reads the URL hash and triggers a click on an element, which gives execution through an auto-clicker. The speaker says a real engagement had gone uncaught by roughly ten years of annual tests.

For defence, the talk recommends context-aware encoding and treating client-side input as untrusted, including in front-end code. Sanitising libraries such as DOMPurify can help, though the speaker notes DOMPurify has had its own vulnerabilities. Content Security Policy reduces risk but can be bypassed in some circumstances. The labs are published on GitHub so practitioners can work through the source-to-sink method themselves.

talks.title: Examining Access Control Vulnerabilities In GraphQL - A Field Case Study
talks.teaser: Examining Access Control Vulnerabilities In GraphQL - A Field Case Study.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Bogdan, co-founder and senior pentester at Forbridge, presents a security case study examining access control vulnerabilities discovered in the dating app Feeld (formerly known as 3nder / Trender). The research identified eight access control vulnerabilities spanning GraphQL and REST endpoints—specifically seven Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) flaws and one Broken Object Property Level Authorization (BOPLA) flaw. These issues enabled unauthorized access to sensitive user data, interception and manipulation of private communications, and complete tampering with user interactions.

### Key Topics
- **OWASP Top 10 Context:** Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) ranks as the #1 threat in the OWASP Top 10 API Security, while Broken Access Control holds the #1 spot in the OWASP Top 10 Web Application Security (2021).
- **Application Background:** Feeld launched in 2014 as 3nder/Trender before rebranding in 2016 due to trademark conflicts. It operates as an alternative dating app with over 1 million Android downloads, catering to specific dating preferences, relationship types, and kink exploration.
- **Access Control Breakdown:** The app relied heavily on client-side restrictions and predictable identifiers, lacking adequate server-side authorization checks on both GraphQL queries/mutations and RESTful endpoints.

### Technical Details
The presentation details eight distinct vulnerabilities discovered within Feeld:

1. **Profile Data Disclosure to Non-Premium Users:** Basic users typically see blurred profile pictures and limited profile data for users who liked them. However, by intercepting the `likesQuery` GraphQL operation in a proxy (Burp Suite), unblurred image URLs hosted on Cloudinary (`cloudinary.com`) and full profile details—including unique `stream_user_id` values—are returned directly in the response unauthenticated.
2. **Reading Private Messages:** Using a victim's `stream_user_id` harvested from the discovery menu, an attacker could supply this ID to the `/channels` endpoint, removing other parameters, to retrieve the victim's complete private chat history.
3. **Accessing Sensitive Media Attachments:** While the app claimed to offer time-limited (15-second) and play-once media, media files were hosted on external CDNs (`api.cloudinary.com` and `streamiocdn.com`). Attackers could leak the direct CDN URLs authenticated or unauthenticated:
   - For replayable images, the backend chat attachment endpoint verified only that an image ID existed, ignoring user identity. Prepending `/v1` to the path exposed the unauthenticated Cloudinary URL directly.
   - For time-limited images (using `visibility_milliseconds: 15000`), attackers could retrieve media via the sender profile ID even after expiration on the receiver's end, or prepend `/v1` to leak the original URL.
   - For videos, direct CDN links in attachment JSON payloads contained unicode-escaped ampersands (`\u0026`), which when unescaped allowed unauthenticated viewing regardless of "play once" limitations.
4. **Deleting, Recovering, and Editing Other People's Messages:** Using a target message ID:
   - Sending an HTTP `DELETE` to `/messages/{message_id}` on an already deleted message recovered the original deleted text.
   - Sending an HTTP `PUT` request with a modified body allowed an attacker to overwrite any user's message with an "edited" flag, obscuring the author's true identity.
5. **Updating Other Users' Profile Information:** The GraphQL mutation `profileUpdate` accepted arbitrary profile IDs, allowing an authenticated user to alter the name, bio, sexuality, and age of other profiles.
6. **Forging Profile Likes:** The GraphQL `profileLike` operation permitted an attacker logged into Account A to forge a like between Account B and Account C, manipulating user match systems.
7. **Injecting Messages into Third-Party Chats:** Attackers could POST messages to `/channels/messaging/{channel_id}/message` without being chat participants. Combined with Feeld's non-unique display names, attackers could trivially impersonate participants.
8. **Viewing Other Users' Matches:** Changing the profile ID parameter in the `chatListQuery` GraphQL operation returned the full match list and associated profile details of any targeted victim.

### Takeaways
- **Developers:** Enforce authorization and role-based access controls strictly on the back end, never relying on the client application to obscure or filter data. Restrict API responses strictly to data appropriate for the requester's tier.
- **DevSecOps:** Incorporate automated API security checks into CI/CD pipelines, noting that manual testing remains essential because automated scanners often struggle to discern access control boundaries among similar GUIDs.
- **CISOs & Leadership:** Perform comprehensive data mapping to locate all collected personal data, apply robust encryption and testing, and monitor third-party storage to prevent regulatory breaches (such as GDPR enforcement actions).
- **Disclosure:** Despite the simplicity of the root causes, Feeld took over six months to remediate all reported issues before public disclosure by the researchers and coverage by outlets like The Guardian.

talks.title: Reviewing COBOL For Fun And Profit
talks.teaser: Coverage of Reviewing COBOL For Fun And Profit from the conference program.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, a former financial sector software developer turned penetration tester and security consultant explains how to approach security code reviews for legacy COBOL applications running on mainframes. Despite modern perceptions that mainframes and COBOL are obsolete relics, they remain central to financial institutions for vital batch operations, overnight routines, and processing massive monetary transactions. The speaker highlights that COBOL is deceptively simple and readable, and that long-standing systems running untouched for decades often harbor overlooked security flaws due to historical operating assumptions.

### Key Topics
- **Mainframes in Modern Finance**: Why organizations maintain mainframes—highlighting high processing power, multi-threading capabilities, and the massive financial and operational costs associated with replacing them.
- **COBOL Architecture & Readability**: An introduction to COBOL's structure (Identification Division, Environment Division, Data Division, and Procedure Division) and its readable, English-like syntax designed originally to eliminate programming mistakes.
- **Shift in Security Assumptions**: Historical perimeter security relied on physically locked rooms, fixed terminal input lengths, and trusted internal networks. Modern attack vectors like cleartext network interception, input manipulation, and updated frontends break these assumptions.
- **Static Analysis Tooling**: Practical tips on requesting raw source files rather than mainframe terminal access, utilizing commercial tools like Checkmarx and Veracode, and using VCG (Visual Code Grepper), an open-source tool authored by the speaker that automates checking COBOL code.

### Technical Details
- **Variable Type & Length Mismatches**: COBOL defines fields like alphanumeric (`PIC X`), numeric (`PIC 9`), and signed numeric (`PIC S9`). When variables of differing lengths or types are copied to one another, COBOL does not generate traditional memory overwrites or C-style overflows; it silently truncates values or coerces characters into numbers. For example, moving a longer monetary value into a shorter variable truncates digits, creating financial discrepancies.
- **SQL Injection in COBOL**: Using the `ACCEPT` statement to collect user input and concatenating it directly into dynamic SQL queries executed against DB2 databases leads directly to SQL injection. DB2's support for semicolon-delimited queries and comment characters enables attackers to execute arbitrary statements.
- **Buffer Overflows & Stack Handling**: Unlike C/C++, COBOL does not interleave instruction pointers on a general-purpose stack alongside data. Overflowing or truncating variables alters application data but does not permit direct execution hijack or overwriting return addresses. The speaker notes the availability of an `ON OVERFLOW` handling routine to capture mismatch conditions.
- **Control Flow Quirks**: Legacy code frequently relies on nested `GO TO` statements and even self-modifying code via constructs like `ALTER PROC1 PROCEED TO PROC2`, which dynamically rewrites jump destinations and produces hard-to-trace spaghetti logic.

### Takeaways
Reviewers should obtain raw code files to analyze with proper tooling rather than wrestling with mainframe terminal interfaces. Client reporting requires explaining risks that have not failed yet but will as variables outgrow legacy capacities (e.g., due to inflation) or as network-level attackers bypass terminal restrictions. Ensuring source libraries on mainframes are execute-only, properly documenting legacy gotos, and verifying that program IDs match filenames are critical remediation steps.

talks.title: "We're In... Jail".A Collection Of Stories Of Cyber Criminals Failing To Crime by Scott McGready
talks.teaser: Stories expose criminals who left phishing data in plain text and confessed to hacks during hours of public live gaming chat.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a lighthearted warning not to commit crime, then walks through cases where offenders made basic operational mistakes. Early examples include phishing kits that left victim lists and kit archives on open web paths, often seeding demo records with the operators’ own details. A misconfigured cloud bucket tied to a Russian dating rival exposed romance scammers who used the same platform to coordinate with each other, ordering food, rides, and flights to real addresses while extorting users.

The centerpiece is the 2017 compromise of the Metropolitan Police Twitter account through a third-party press-desk tool, followed by tweets that were juvenile rather than destructive. Investigation leaned on open-source clues, a long public live stream where associates discussed the breach, and physical traces such as Wi-Fi names from proof videos. The speaker contrasts heavy-handed prosecution under the Computer Misuse Act with the low severity of the harm.

Later anecdotes cover reporting tens of thousands of stolen card rows to confused local police, a brief Crime Stoppers volunteer stint that ended after a weak session cookie granted admin access, and a more constructive force that thanked a researcher who could order every bike on an insecure seized-goods site. The close urges hackers and law enforcement to bridge cultural gaps instead of treating each other as opposites.

talks.title: An Offensive Perspective Of Ransomware Operations by Chris Truncer
talks.teaser: Walks through ransomware group tradecraft and recreated tooling, then shows which basic defenses make attacker life harder.
talks.summary:
This talk takes an offensive look at how several ransomware groups operate, drawing on incident response write-ups and the tools those groups were seen using. The speaker argues that much of their tradecraft is basic rather than sophisticated. He and a colleague rebuilt some of the observed tooling, such as ping-based host discovery, a PowerShell domain computer enumeration script and a simple encrypted shellcode loader, so it could be used for emulation and testing.

One group tied to Cuba ransomware ran double extortion, encrypting data and also stealing it and posting samples on a leak site. It got in mainly through exploitation of Exchange flaws from the ProxyLogon and ProxyShell period, then used web shells, a NetSupport RAT, Mimikatz and batch scripts that opened every drive to all users. A second group relied on initial access brokers and phishing with password-protected archives. Its loaders disguised RC4-encrypted shellcode as image files, and it installed backdoors through Inno Setup installers. It also used Unicode-escaped commands to slip past detections. The time from initial access to ransomware deployment dropped from about five and a half days in July 2020 to about one and a half days by October.

The speaker says endpoint tools alone are not enough and that layered controls matter. His practical suggestions include application allowlisting, which he found to be the hardest control to get past, canary tokens and deception accounts that raise alerts when touched, network segmentation, removing unnecessary admin rights, and regular red team or penetration testing. He also recommends command-line auditing and testing whether odd command patterns trigger any alerts.

talks.title: Nuclear Hack Simulation With Airbus Protects CyberRange by Nathan Pooley
talks.teaser: An OT specialist covers nuclear CNI basics, then runs a cyber-range demo from phishing to firewall and PLC compromise.
talks.summary:
Operational technology in nuclear and other critical national infrastructure reverses familiar IT priorities: safety and availability outweigh confidentiality, and decades-old mechanical controls may never carry passwords. The talk surveys PLCs, HMIs, engineering workstations, SCADA and ICS terminology, UK nuclear regulation and NCSC initiatives such as the industry expert community, and IEC 62443 security levels derived from zone risk assessments. It also covers the Purdue reference model and zone-and-conduit rules that govern how traffic may cross OT boundaries.

The presenter describes Airbus Protect’s cyber range as an on-site platform that virtualizes customer firewalls, PLC configurations, and traffic captures so teams can pentest and train without destabilizing live plant timing. In a scripted nuclear exercise, initial access comes from a phishing compromise of a remote user’s VPN credentials, followed by automated scanning, exploitation of a long-unpatched perimeter firewall, and modification of legacy plain-text PLC traffic that forces rapid pump failover. The simulation shows rising outage costs, cooling failures, and hazardous reactor indicators while the mock CISO cites neglected risk entries and staffing choices.

Audiences should leave understanding why OT sites resist classic IT hardening, how digital-twin ranges support compliant testing, and which segmentation, patching, and training gaps turn marginal VPN footholds into physical process impact.

talks.title: Hunting For Bugs That Scanners Miss, And WAFs Fail To Detect by Ayoub Safa
talks.teaser: Shows how mobile app traffic, predictable UUIDs and shared JWT secrets expose bugs that scanners and WAFs overlook.
talks.summary:
The talk covers web application and API vulnerabilities that automated scanners and web application firewalls often miss. The speaker argues that testers should look beyond a site's JavaScript files and also examine its mobile apps, since those apps can call backend endpoints the web front end never loads. In one case, an endpoint reached through a mobile app accepted the same credentials as the login flow without enforcing the second factor. In another, a simple Boolean SQL injection was reachable only through the mobile interface.

The middle of the talk covers authorization and token weaknesses. One case involved an indirect variant of insecure direct object reference, where a background request tied the victim's asset to the attacker's account and could be replayed. The speaker then explains that UUID version 1 values embed a timestamp and the MAC address of the generating machine. An attacker who knows roughly when a password reset token was created can therefore generate candidate values and guess the victim's token. A further case involved JSON Web Tokens whose payload held only an integer user ID and whose signing secret was shared between staging and production. Accounts created on staging yielded IDs matching real production users, which exposed more than 12,000 accounts.

For practitioners, the takeaways are to include mobile apps when enumerating endpoints, to keep signing keys separate for each environment, and to avoid sequential IDs or email addresses as token identifiers. Identifiers should be random version 4 UUIDs, and email ownership should be verified before trusting an account.

talks.title: The Non-Tech Stuff I Wasn't Prepared For by Ian Davies
talks.teaser: A security generalist outlines listening, communication, negotiation, and business skills practitioners need beyond technical work.
talks.summary:
The presenter describes a move from technical architecture and infrastructure work into an in-house security generalist role at a European building-supply group. The session argues that information security holds many skilled roles beyond hands-on engineering, and that capabilities such as listening, critical thinking, and communication matter across GRC, incident response, testing, and architecture.

The bulk of the talk walks through practical habits: active listening without interrupting or invalidating others; thinking clearly when decisions must land in short meetings; explaining risks and pen-test findings in plain language to marketing and other non-IT owners; negotiating trade-offs between security and operability; pacing change incrementally rather than demanding instant compliance; reading business goals, budgets, and vendor quotes; lightweight project management across distributed teams; and catching detail errors that can undermine reports. Community suggestions extend into psychology, empathy, humor, and using office tools such as Excel for recurring security outputs.

The close frames security as a people-centered field where technology protects livelihoods and well-being. The speaker invites disagreement or agreement during questions, positioning the material as personal lessons from shifting away from purely technical delivery.

talks.title: "You Missed A Period Don't Panic" Why Words Matter by Alice McGready
talks.teaser: Shows how word choice and audience shape compliance answers, on-call escalation, and professional security writing.
talks.summary:
Alice McGready argues that security practitioners solve puzzles with language as much as with tools, and that shared English still fails when writers ignore who will read or hear a message. She opens from publishing and Cyber Essentials work, using a ambiguous questionnaire answer to show how one missing punctuation mark can flip meaning and stall assessments.

Through pop-culture and workplace vignettes, she compares ineffective long stories with blunt incident openers, contrasts reports written for peers with what executives or clients need, and cautions against formal salutations, careless social posts, unexplained acronyms, and U.S. versus U.K. wording traps. A live edit of a real CV profile demonstrates trimming generic claims, foregrounding what motivates the candidate, and choosing positive, team-oriented phrasing.

She closes with practical habits: rehearsing a lightning-length core message, keeping style guides, auditing personal verbal tics, being deliberate with dates in reusable content, structuring arguments clearly, and using simple reference lookups. The intended takeaway is to put facts and priorities first for each stakeholder so technical knowledge actually lands.

talks.title: Decoding The Maze Of Malware Detection by Sarah White
talks.teaser: Shows how transfer learning on image renderings of malware binaries can sort samples into malware types.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the problem that thousands of new malware samples appear every day, which makes hand-written signatures impractical. It gives a primer on artificial intelligence, machine learning and its three main approaches, then explains neural networks and why convolutional neural networks suit image-like input. Transfer learning is presented as a way to reuse a network pretrained on natural images and fine-tune it on malware images.

The project converted Windows executables into grayscale and RGB images, removed corrupt files and very small or low-detection samples, and labelled each file by its most common detection type. Installer and packed categories were dropped, and the final model reached a mean accuracy of 91.2 percent, with precision, recall and F1 each around 0.9. Per-class accuracy ranged from 84.9 percent for crypto miners to 96.9 percent for the best class, and smaller, more uniform classes tended to score higher.

The speaker noted that related papers reported higher scores but used much smaller datasets, and that separating malware types is harder than separating malware from benign files. Suggested next steps included training a model from scratch, collecting benign and newer samples, and using explainability to show which parts of a file drive a decision. The main takeaway is that enough samples per class matters as much as the choice of model.

talks.title: Beyond Microsoft IIS Short File Name Disclosure by Soroush Dalili
talks.teaser: Explores IIS short file name disclosure from manual OPTIONS probes through automation and mapping shorts to real filenames.
talks.summary:
The presentation revisits Microsoft IIS short file name (8.3) disclosure, a issue the speaker reported around 2010 that Microsoft still classifies as a bug rather than a vulnerability. It explains how legacy FAT-style names are generated on modern Windows, why they remain enabled by default, and how HTTP handling in IIS exposes them when paths use tilde-digit patterns, wildcards, and framework-specific URL suffixes.

The core technique relies on response differences—often a flip between 200 and 404 when using the OPTIONS method instead of blocked GET wildcards—and character-by-character guessing with asterisk and question-mark semantics. The speaker walks through manual tab-based testing, Burp Intruder cluster-bomb setups, verification against known files such as web.config, and workarounds when OPTIONS is blocked or characters are filtered. He compares his long-standing Java scanner with newly released tools that extend enumeration to full names via rainbow tables and CRC-style hex short names, plus tips on alternate data streams, probing bin contents, distinguishing applications from virtual directories, and enumerating entire long filenames when a tilde and digit appear anywhere in the path.

Practitioners are urged to treat recovered short names as starting points: map them to real names via sitemaps, dorks, dictionaries, or cautious use of generative assistants, while understanding rate limits and WAF blocking. Defense starts with disabling short-name creation on freshly provisioned hosts before content is deployed, but the speaker stresses that obscurity is insufficient—sensitive files need proper access controls regardless.

talks.title: How Being A Javascript CTF Challenge Creator Has Helped Me At Reverse-Engineering by Maya Boeckh
talks.teaser: Shows how JavaScript obfuscation built for CTF challenges helps unpick a phishing kit's anti-analysis layers.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker's background in capture-the-flag events as a player and challenge creator. Building a challenge follows the same steps each time: have an idea, check feasibility, make it reproducible, keep it approachable and document it. The speaker then walks through JSFuck, a style of JavaScript written with only six characters. Starting from values such as false, true, undefined and Infinity, the speaker shows how to extract letters and numbers, reach the Function constructor, and build strings that execute as code.

The middle section looks at the kinds of challenges the speaker has written, including a text box that evaluates input, pseudo-random number generators, data hidden in images and audio, and base128 encoding. The main lesson is that browser code runs at runtime, so a debugger breakpoint reveals decoded logic even when it is obfuscated. A case study follows: a phishing campaign a friend asked about, with a redirect chain, a payload decoded by a custom routine and then evaluated, and anti-analysis checks. Those checks fingerprint browser features such as workers, iframes and canvas before choosing between a login page and a sinkhole.

The closing advice is that obfuscation only slows analysis down and that anything placed in front-end code should be treated as exposed. Renaming or removing eval, tracing the code at runtime and mapping the fingerprinting stage are practical ways to dissect such pages. The speaker also notes that some JSFuck-style XSS payloads can slip past web application firewalls, so input handling should not depend on a filter alone.

talks.title: Adversaries Have It Easy. Live FAFO Pnwing A Network by Andy Gill & Neil Lines
talks.teaser: A live progression releases AD offensive tools and chains credential reuse, share abuse, and shadow credentials to domain compromise.
talks.summary:
The presenters frame a red-team style engagement against a fictional virtual-reality company: open-source intelligence surfaces leaked credentials, and a single-factor SSL VPN portal grants internal access. Much of the session is a deliberately manual, live progression through post-VPN footholds rather than a polished automation pipeline.

They demonstrate a suite they call offensive sysadmin tooling—SlinkyCat for fast LDAP and ADSI enumeration (including risky checks such as user descriptions mentioning passwords and attempts to mount the C$ share), SharpShares for mapping readable SMB shares as a standard domain user, Domain Scrape for keyword searches across mounted shares, and SharpCreds for harvesting users and matching a chosen password against lockout policy. They also reference Scraping Kit for controller and Outlook COM keyword harvesting, though several live runs fail or return little in a freshly rebuilt lab. The arc culminates in shadow credentials: using Whisker (and Ruby’s for Kerberos) to add an MS Key Credential, obtain a certificate from Active Directory Certificate Services, pass the ticket, and reach domain-controller–level access, with discussion of DC Sync, DPAPI keys, and operational rollback cautions.

Practitioners hear that mature organizations still leak credentials in shares and descriptions, that PowerShell remains viable in many estates, and that detection is hard because LDAP and share abuse exploit intended features. The tools are positioned for release with a blog post and prior workshop lab guidance for hands-on practice.

talks.title: Delivering The Fail, The Post Office IT Scandal by Brian Whelton
talks.teaser: A session recounts the Horizon scandal, wrongful prosecutions, and disclosures exposing Post Office and Fujitsu failures.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames how everyday reliance on computer-recorded evidence intersects with UK criminal procedure, including the shift away from requiring proof that systems worked correctly before their output could be used in court. It then walks through the Post Office’s Horizon platform—marketed as robust while sub-postmasters running franchised branches were told shortfalls on screen were their fault, often after being pushed to “settle” discrepancies so they could trade the next day.

The middle of the session stacks public and leaked material: Fujitsu defect trackers spanning huge page counts, admissions that remote support could alter live data without adequate logging, independent Second Sight reviews the Post Office tried to contain, and civil group litigation culminating in Justice Fraser’s 2019 judgment. It contrasts that technical record with prosecutions driven in-house, investigators treating missing balances as theft without tracing funds, and expert witnesses tied to the vendor. Cases such as Lee Castleton’s civil fight and Seema Misra’s imprisonment illustrate aggressive litigation spend and withheld bug context.

Practitioners are urged to treat vendor assertions, audit screens, and “computer says so” narratives as testable claims—not substitutes for logs, change control, and disclosure. The arc ends with hundreds of convictions overturned or under review, police inquiries into witness conduct, and a continuing statutory inquiry, with pointers to books, journalism, and primary documents so teams can study governance, integrity, and legal process failures together.

talks.title: 2019 LT: Novel VM Detection Tricks
talks.teaser: Coverage of 2019 LT: Novel VM Detection Tricks from the conference program.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, a security researcher from Nettitude's Research and Innovation (R&I) team presents novel and user-mode techniques for detecting virtual machines (VMs) on Windows systems. Building on earlier research and contributions to the open-source tool 'al-khaser' (maintained primarily by LordNoteworthy), the speaker explores how hypervisors fail to accurately emulate real physical hardware, creating distinct forensic footprints that malware authors, red teams, and security analysts can leverage.

### Key Topics
- **Design Constraints of al-khaser**: The speaker details the strict operating rules used for the al-khaser project: zero custom or vulnerable kernel drivers (avoiding driver-signing hurdles and system compromise), no exploit-based breakouts, no modification of system settings, and pure user-mode C++ implementations for Windows.
- **ACPI Firmware Table Inspection**: Utilizing Windows user-mode APIs like `EnumSystemFirmwareTables` to inspect ACPI tables, SMBIOS data, and missing firmware signatures (e.g., absence of HPET or WPBT tables, presence of vendor strings like 'VMware').
- **Direct ATA Commands**: Interacting with physical hard drives via ATA IDENTIFY commands to pinpoint inconsistent flags, obsolete SCSI versions, or hardcoded emulation artifacts.
- **PCI Bus and Power Management Artifacts**: Identifying repetitive virtual PCI topologies and hypervisor omissions such as nonexistent ACPI sleep states (S1–S4).
- **WMI Hardware Querying**: Probing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for missing physical components, such as temperature sensors, fans, and voltage probes.

### Technical Details
- **ACPI Tables and Firmware Quirks**: Real modern hardware consistently contains High Precision Event Timers (HPET) and vendor licensing tables (SLIC), whereas VMs generally omit them. Furthermore, SMBIOS binaries in virtual environments frequently leak default vendor strings directly in memory, such as 'VMware 2006'.
- **Direct Disk Querying (`ATA IDENTIFY`)**: Running the `ATA IDENTIFY` command via the `DeviceIoControl` API against physical disk handles exposes inconsistencies in virtual device controllers (e.g., VirtualBox returning conflicting capability flags where features are reported unsupported yet enabled). Furthermore, virtualized platforms often emulate archaic interfaces (like 1993-era SCSI) never found on modern physical systems. The speaker created a helper tool called `ata_identify_dump` to map these anomalies across hypervisors.
- **PCI Topologies**: Using SetupAPIs and WMI, user-mode applications can inspect PCI routes, multiplexers, and vendor/device IDs. Hypervisors (VirtualBox, VMware, Hyper-V) share predictable, hardcoded virtual PCI device layouts.
- **Sleep States (`GetPwrCapabilities`)**: Hypervisors rarely implement physical power management. Calling `GetPwrCapabilities` reveals that ACPI sleep states S1, S2, S3, and S4 are entirely unsupported on almost all virtualization platforms.
- **WMI Inconsistencies**: User-mode queries against WMI reveal fake CPU cache sizes, fixed memory array configurations, and a complete absence of thermal zones, fan controllers, and voltage probes.

### Takeaways
Hardware emulation in hypervisors focuses on functional minimums rather than absolute parity with physical hardware. As a result, virtual environments can be reliably detected entirely from user mode without specialized kernel privileges or exploits. While user-mode API hooking and hypervisor updates can attempt to mask these signs, emulating every physical quirk remains a persistent cat-and-mouse challenge.

talks.title: 2019 LT: People Are The Solution!
talks.teaser: Coverage of 2019 LT: People Are The Solution! from the conference program.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this lightning talk titled "People Are The Solution!", a cybersecurity senior lecturer addresses the cultural and communication issues prevalent within the information security industry. Drawing on global demographic statistics, cybersecurity workforce estimates, and common security attitudes, the speaker argues against the pervasive industry habit of dismissing end users and developers as "idiots." Instead, the presentation makes the case that security professionals must recognize the scale of the challenge, stop treating others poorly, and focus on helping people make fewer mistakes through supportive technology, proper training, and empathy.

### Key Topics
- **Cybersecurity Demographics and Workforce Disparity**: The speaker opens with a quiz contrasting the 2018 world population (7.5 billion from the US Census) and estimated breach records (5.09 billion) against the roughly 6 million cybersecurity workers worldwide. Security personnel represent under 0.08% of the global population, demonstrating the massive numerical disadvantage security teams face against devices and breaches.
- **The Flaw of Blaming Users**: Referencing a comment attributed to the CTO of Amazon stating that "there's always that idiot that will click the link," the speaker critiques the habit of calling users idiots. Insulting users alienates them, causes them to ignore security advice, and overlooks the fact that phishing lures are explicitly designed to deceive.
- **The Role of Security Professionals**: Security's core mission is framed as helping users make fewer mistakes through thoughtful technology implementation and training—moving away from ineffective, unengaging slide-based training.
- **Professional Conduct and Empathy ("Don't Be a Dick")**: The speaker urges practitioners to monitor how they treat colleagues. If a user's only interaction with security is negative, they assume the entire profession is hostile. A suggested core policy for security teams is simply to avoid acting poorly toward others.
- **Empathy for Developers and Humility**: Practitioners are urged to stay humble and remember that no one started out as a security expert. Developers often release insecure code not out of incompetence, but due to intense business pressures, buyouts, or simply not being taught practices like input sanitization.

### Technical Details
- **Population vs. Breach Data**: Data cited includes a world population of 7.5 billion (2018 US Census data), 5.09 billion estimated breached records, and an estimated 6 million global cybersecurity workforce (representing less than 0.08% of the population).
- **Phishing and User Design**: The talk emphasizes that phishing links are engineered to fool human targets; even experienced security professionals (such as a referenced Data Protection Officer, Carl Gottlieb) can come close to clicking on malicious links.
- **Development Pitfalls**: Mentions common security fundamentals such as input sanitization and explains that developers facing downward financial deadlines or legacy practices ("we've always done it that way for 20 years") may introduce vulnerabilities unintentionally.

### Takeaways
- Calling end users or colleagues "idiots" fails as a security strategy and only drives disengagement.
- The primary job of cybersecurity professionals is to support people and minimize errors through better training, supportive technology, and empathetic communication.
- Professionals should remain humble, remembering that everyone started knowing nothing, and recognize the external constraints under which software developers and users operate.

talks.title: 2019 LT: The Problem With DNS
talks.teaser: Explains DNS's missing security, from cache poisoning and amplification attacks to encrypted DNS options like DoT and DoH.
talks.summary:
This lightning talk looks at why the Domain Name System is a weak point in internet security. DNS translates names into IP addresses by moving a query through a chain of root servers, top-level domain servers, registrars and resolvers. The protocol was designed without encryption, authentication or integrity checks, so anyone on the path between a client and its resolver can read or change the answers.

The speaker traces how DNSSEC was added over many years, with early attempts in the 1990s needing revision and a full redesign by 2005. A flaw found by Dan Kaminsky showed that resolver caches could be poisoned because transaction IDs were too limited, and the speaker says only about a quarter of resolvers validate DNSSEC today. The talk then covers amplification: by spoofing source addresses, a small query can draw a much larger response aimed at a victim. The speaker's own lab test generated over 150 megabits of traffic. Response rate limiting and forcing large answers over TCP are presented as mitigations.

The final section covers encrypted alternatives. DNS over TLS was standardised through the DPRIVE working group from 2014, and DNS over HTTPS was promoted by Google and Mozilla. Android 9 added private DNS support. The speaker points out that encryption complicates DNS filtering used by schools, banks and ISPs, and that running an internal resolver on something like a Raspberry Pi is a practical option. The talk ends with links to specifications and guides.

talks.title: 2019: How Not To Be As Stupid As Ransomware Authors
talks.teaser: Walks through real ransomware families' cryptographic mistakes, from key reuse to leaked keys, and what developers should avoid.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a primer on cryptography: plaintext and ciphertext, symmetric and public-key ciphers, stream versus block ciphers, and block modes such as ECB, which leaks patterns, compared with modes that use an initialization vector. It also covers pseudo-random and true random number generators and why seeding and insecure generators matter.

The speaker then walks through ransomware families that got these details wrong. Early low-effort strains only renamed files, while one custom XOR-style scheme let a single known plaintext and ciphertext pair reveal its key in seconds. Others kept static keys inside the executable, derived keys from machine details, or used a weak random generator that left only about four billion possible keys. Key reuse with a stream cipher let one recovered keystream unlock many files, and a shared campaign key meant one victim's private key could decrypt others. A Windows-based family left its RSA key pairs on disk because a flag was missing from sample code, and another leaked its private key by rearranging ECB blocks in its key file.

The closing advice is to avoid rolling your own cryptography, avoid copying code you do not understand, and read documentation carefully. Developers should choose well-reviewed, easy-to-use libraries, match block modes and key handling to the cipher, and use a strong source of randomness. The speaker also stresses that infrastructure matters as much as the algorithm, and that victims without good backups may still face paying the ransom.

talks.title: 2019: Rage Against The FUD - The Beer Farmers
talks.teaser: Exposes security marketing built on fear, uncertainty, and doubt, with lessons on disclosure, certs, and peer support.
talks.summary:
The presenters open by defining fear, uncertainty, and doubt as emotional and cognitive levers that skew choices, from sextortion scams to product pitches. They walk through recent community battles over “unhackable” claims, contrasting publicity with hands-on findings on devices such as the Bitfi wallet, and they skewer allied hype from figures whose credibility does not match their marketing.

The middle of the session ties misleading vendor narratives to real incidents practitioners know well: false links between British Airways fines and certificate types, overstated value of extended validation and domain warranty products, blockchain and “next generation” branding with little substance, and alarmist machine-learning promises. They argue for accurate facts in sales material and note browser trends toward treating HTTPS as baseline rather than a special badge.

They close on human costs and process. Cyber work is stressful; public pile-ons on Twitter are a poor substitute for panel conversations on mental health and diversity. On disclosure, they favor sustained vendor engagement when possible, but highlight cases—from Motorola routing issues to abrupt zero-day releases—where users suffer when coordination fails. Hiring hype, certification mismatches, fines that flow to treasury rather than defenders, NHS technical debt, and WannaCry as collateral damage round out a plea to prioritize maintainable systems and community support over theater.

talks.teaser: Shares practical lessons on selective alerting, appliance sprawl, insider risk and incident planning for blue teams.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that many defenders still make avoidable mistakes in how they run security operations. It starts with logging: collecting everything helps forensics, but blue teams need selective alerts built from combined events and tuned regularly to cut false positives. One story describes a firewall setup that logged suspicious traffic without blocking it and without anyone reviewing the logs.

Security appliances should be tools inside a wider toolchain, and unused ones should be powered off, since each is another path into the network. A proof-of-concept device phoned home to its vendor and produced little of value. For devices that cannot be patched, such as certified medical equipment, virtual patching at a web application firewall is an imperfect but better-than-nothing fallback. Physical access matters too, shown by a backup data centre whose door was propped open with a stone.

Teams should agree a written, company-approved incident plan that names who decides, who informs and who handles the media. Blame should give way to finding root causes, knowledge should be shared rather than held by one enthusiastic expert, and staff should learn basic habits such as locking screens. When budgets or people are short, open-source tools can fill gaps if the team has time to run them. The speaker closes by urging anyone unable to change anything at work to consider moving on.

talks.title: 2019: How The Equation Group Remained Out Of Sight Over The Years
talks.teaser: Traces how the Equation Group's KillSuit framework installs, persists through a bootkit, and can be detected and removed.
talks.summary:
The talk examines KillSuit, a post-exploitation framework from the Equation Group that was leaked by the Shadow Brokers in 2017 and is loosely linked to the NSA. Its modules offer man-in-the-middle redirection, full packet capture, Wi-Fi exfiltration from air-gapped machines, and custom TCP/IP stacks that avoid the Windows networking API.

Installation left several indicators. The implant repeatedly checked a setup-in-progress registry value, and its hashing calls inside a calculator process were anomalous. Each installation also wrote encrypted module records under randomized 32-character registry paths built from two combined lists, which the team could not recover from the binaries because of anti-debugging and runtime protections. A cryptographic provider type 23, absent from Microsoft's default list, appeared on first installation and served as a consistent marker. For persistence, the bootkit variant that worked up to Windows 7 rewrote the master and volume boot records, hid its kernel driver inside a TrueType font file located through an NTFS object ID index, and checked its integrity before handing control to the boot manager.

For detection, the team wrote a check that flagged unexpected no-operation bytes in boot records before a jump, which identified every bootkit installation they tested. Removing the encrypted registry database disabled the running modules and the bootkit's dependency on them. Firmware-level persistence was harder to address, and Secure Boot on UEFI systems and Windows 8 and later blocked the boot-record changes. The main takeaway is to hunt for registry artifacts and boot record anomalies.

talks.teaser: Shows how to build and deploy Windows Defender Application Control policies, and how attackers can work around them.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Windows Defender Application Control, an allow-list feature included with Windows 10 Enterprise and Server 2016 at no extra cost, formerly called Device Guard. The speaker explains how code integrity policies decide what may load, covering applications and drivers, and why most rules rely on digital signatures. Policies are written as XML, converted to a binary format, and can run in audit mode to log what would have been blocked without enforcing anything. Unsigned software needs catalog files, which must be regenerated after each update.

Two policy-building strategies are compared. A gold-image scan records whatever is installed on a workstation, but it can trust Microsoft binaries known to enable allow-list bypasses, and a scan on a nearly empty system took about three days. A default-deny approach starts from an empty policy in audit mode and adds rules from audit event logs using the audit flag and merge commands. A demo then shows deploying the binary policy through a Group Policy setting that points to a readable share, and confirming it through the policy file in the system code integrity folder and event ID 7010.

On the offensive side, the speaker notes that constrained language mode restricts PowerShell, yet a WMI-based tool still starts processes, moves files and returns command output while the policy is enforced. Blocking WMI is one possible defense. The talk closes by suggesting enforcement begin on fixed-function systems such as ATMs and domain controllers, using audit telemetry to justify wider rollout.

talks.title: 2019: Dragon
talks.teaser: Shows how phishing, captured SMB credentials and macro payloads let a red team reach domain admin.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the December 2015 power outage in Ukraine, attributed to the Dragonfly group, and the speaker's interest in how such actors steal credentials through spear phishing. A single SMB request embedded in a web page's index file can make a visiting Internet Explorer user send a username, domain and password hash to an attacker's listener. Stolen mail access through OWA can also be used to upload and trigger a reverse shell, and the speaker notes that some APT groups have started using the same approach.

The middle section follows a red team engagement. A phishing email leads to a macro-enabled Word document, which gives remote access to a workstation. A local administrator hash found there is reused across cloned machines, because the same local password hash is often shared, and passing the hash grants access to other hosts. A domain administrator's cleartext password is then recovered from a Windows Server 2008 host. The speaker also covers Unicorn payloads, PowerShell one-liners that were later caught by signatures, and how AMSI and Defender affect them. Limits on VBA line continuations led to a converter that turns PowerShell into macro code, which requests service account Kerberos tickets and emails the results.

The closing part chains these steps into a single click, and checks passwords stored in the user description field in Active Directory. The speaker argues that mature organisations can still be compromised through reused credentials, legacy Windows 7 and XP systems, and weak macro controls, while Windows 10 with Defender is harder to attack. Defenders should prioritise credential exposure, unique local admin passwords and retiring legacy systems.

The session marks the closing remarks of the SteelCon 2018 cybersecurity conference. Led by members of the organizing team (including Mike, Neil, and Robin), the presentation serves as a wrap-up to express gratitude to sponsors, staff, speakers, and attendees, while announcing competition winners, charity fundraising numbers, and upcoming post-conference social events.

### Key Topics
- **Sponsor and Venue Acknowledgments**: The organizers thanked MWR (the main sponsor contributing significant funding), Nettitude (sponsoring the evening party, food, lunch, and breakfast), and Sheffield Hallam University for providing the venue.
- **Staff, AV, and Speaker Recognition**: Thanks were extended to the event crew, kids' crew, and volunteer speakers and workshop leaders who donated their time without travel or lodging reimbursement. Special recognition went to Cooper for recording and publishing conference videos, Gemma and Ross (university AV team), and Chris for event photography.
- **Charity Fundraising**: Scott's sticker stall raised £1,100, supported by vendor-donated swag and a notable donation from Wes. A bring-and-buy sale raised £133, and an auction of an ST and an Amiga computer was expected to add around £200 to the total.
- **Competitions and Raffles**: An 18-ticket raffle was held for attendees. Recognition was given to Dean for winning the "Snipers Alley" target-shooting contest, Bethany for winning "Pippa's Logic Challenge" (awarded a choice between a Game Developer Barbie and a £25 Pimoroni voucher), and Gilly for winning the speaker award.
- **Kids Track**: Coordinated by Tanya and crew, the Kids Track included technical and hands-on activities, with three youth participants reportedly winning adult challenges in the atrium.
- **Post-Conference Activities**: Announcements covered the evening party featuring a buffet, PowerPoint karaoke (noted as 18+ content), a live musical performance by Dual Core, beer tokens, and the Sunday morning pub quiz/laser quasar walk, as well as local outdoor activities during Sheffield's Cliffhanger festival.

### Technical Details
As this transcript covers the conference closing ceremonies, it does not include technical security research, vulnerability disclosures, or technical tool presentations. It focuses strictly on event logistics, community fundraising, attendee contests, and social scheduling.

### Takeaways
SteelCon 2018 concluded successfully as a volunteer-driven, community-oriented cybersecurity conference. Attendees were encouraged to participate in post-conference social gatherings, sign a tribute shirt/care package for "plucky monkey" (Mike), and complete the post-event attendee survey to assist with demographic and statistical reporting for future sponsors under GDPR guidelines.

talks.title: 2018 What Does It Take To Steal $81m? by Donato Capitella and Oliver Simonnet
talks.teaser: Consultants map how SWIFT payment heists unfold end to end and why mandated controls still leave realistic attack paths open.
talks.summary:
The presenters frame their work at MWR around the 2016 Bank of Bangladesh incident, where attackers tried to move roughly $1 billion through SWIFT messaging and made off with $81 million. They give a practical overview of how cross-border payments work: banks exchange instruction messages rather than cash, and a member institution runs local components such as the Alliance Gateway, messaging interface, web front end, and relationship controls tied into ordinary IT.

They walk a timeline of publicly reported thefts from Sonali Bank through Ecuador, Vietnam’s trojaned PDF workflow, Bangladesh’s Alliance Access malware and printer manipulation, and later cases in Taiwan and Nepal. The attack pattern they stress is familiar enterprise intrusion—phishing or other footholds, reconnaissance for payment makers and checkers or SWIFT admins, lateral movement to those workstations, tampering with legitimate four-eyes processes, and anti-forensic habits—rather than exotic Swift-only exploits.

They argue that triggering a payment is often easier than laundering proceeds, which demands organized infrastructure and is where many plots fail. Swift’s Customer Security Programme and isolated “secure zones” raise baselines but leave upstream links and static compliance vulnerable to adaptive attackers. They close by recommending attack-path modeling and detection along realistic routes instead of treating frameworks as complete protection, noting criminal focus may shift to systems outside the hardened enclave.

talks.title: 2018 I Wrote My Own Ransomware; Did Not Make 1 Iota Of A Bitcoin by Thomas Fischer
talks.teaser: Follows a researcher's build of a simple test ransomware and how different endpoint detection tools responded to it.
talks.summary:
The talk examines why ransomware exploded around 2016 and what the speaker learned by building a ransomware prototype for internal testing. Campaign data showed weekly waves, zipped JavaScript and Office documents replacing malicious links, and ransomware-as-a-service being sold on the dark web. The speaker sorts ransomware into four tiers, from scripted tools that barely use cryptography up to public-key designs that are costly to run as a business.

The prototype was written in PHP for simplicity, using an older interpreter build to avoid missing libraries. It applied XOR to the first 1024 bytes of selected document and archive types, which kept it fast while still leaving files unusable. After encryption it renamed files, and it added randomized delays between file changes to dodge behaviour-based detection. Delivery used a Word or Excel document with DDE to run a command, and a purchased crimeware kit registered infected machines to a web panel, which showed whether they were real users or sandboxes.

Testing against endpoint products gave uneven results: some tools missed the script until script blocking was enabled, and extension-based rules were easy to sidestep. The whole build took under 24 hours, which the speaker used to argue that the barrier to entry is low. The closing point was human: many victims paid ransoms themselves rather than report a mistake to their employer. Practitioners should watch for bulk file modification patterns and train staff to report incidents early.
